newsitem.title: USA: Record yields boost U.S. wheat outlook.
newsitem.headline: Record yields boost U.S. wheat outlook.

text.p: U.S. winter wheat yields will hit record levels this year despite a hard April freeze that many analysts thought would cripple the crop, the U.S. Agriculture Department said on Friday.
Based on July 1 conditions, the department pegged the U.S. winter wheat harvest at 1.78 billion bushels, up 11 percent from its June estimate and 20 percent from a year ago.
Yields were put at a record 42.8 bushels per acre, up 5.6 bushels from last year.

"Overall the crop is quite significant, in large part because of extraordinary yields," Agriculture Secretary Dan Glickman told reporters. "We have a good crop, a big crop, a high yielding crop and a high quality crop," he said.

The reason for the dramatic turnaround has been the weather since the April frost, which was "nature at its best" for winter wheat, said Fred Vogel, director of the estimates division of USDA's National Agricultural Statistic.
Conditions were so ideal that farmers will harvest 800,000 acres that previously were expected to be abandoned, he said.

Glickman's home state of Kansas is now expected to produce 449.4 million bushels, up from last month's estimate of 363.8 million and last year's output of 255.2 million, which was reduced by drought. The Kansas wheat crop is the largest since the 1982 record of 458.5 million bushels.
Kansas winter wheat yields are now expected to average 42 bushels per acre, up from the department's June estimate of 34 bushels and last year's 29 bushels.
"I've just heard some amazing yield numbers," said Gregg Doud, a grains analyst with Washington-based World Perspectives.
The central corriodor of the hard red winter wheat belt between Enid, Okla., and Beloit, Kan., "really kicked it into gear" after the frost, Doud said.
The department forecast the total U.S. wheat crop at 2.43 billion bushels -- the largest crop in five years.
But Doud said that masks trouble for the U.S. spring wheat crop, which has not had as favourable growing conditions.

Department forecasters lowered their projection of the spring wheat crop to 651 million bushels, from 704 million last month. Much of that reduction is for durum, a hard amber wheat used to make pasta.
That could trigger renewed grain trade tensions with Canada, which the Clinton administration in the past has accused of flooding the U.S. market with cheap imports.
But with U.S. durum output pegged at 81 million bushels, down 30 percent from last year, it will be hard for U.S. pasta makers to get by without importing Canadian durum, Doud said.

Reflecting the durum shortfall, the Agriculture Department raised its estimate of 1997-98 (June-May) U.S. wheat imports to 100 million bushels from its previous estimate of 90 million. Virtually all U.S. wheat imports come from Canada.

Just before 1 p.m. EDT, wheat contracts on the Kansas City and Chicago futures exchanges were trading 1 cent to almost 3 cents lower under the weight of winter wheat estimate, which exceeded most analysts' expectations.
In its report, the Department further reduced its estimate of season-average prices for the 1997 wheat crop to $3.40 per bushel, down 95 cents from last year.
That downward price trend could increase pressure on the USDA to resurrect its wheat export subsidy programme, which has been dormant for nearly two years.
Glickman stopped short of saying the department would take that step. But the big crop "increases our desire to move this wheat as aggressively as we can," he said.
